To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the human brain has the capacity of running in parallel a very large number of cognitive tasks, and (2) the number of parallel tasks is not constant but varies according to the complexity of the task, the activation level and the specific brain region.

(i) the human brain is a complex, multi-dimensional system, and (ii) the number of independent processes running in parallel when performing complex cognitive task can be estimated via data-driven analysis.

(1) the number of independent sources that are activated in the human brain during a complex cognitive task can be estimated using fMRI and (2) the number of these independent sources is a continuous function of the activation level, which can be defined in terms of the fMRI signal amplitude.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of the number of parallel processes that are active in the human brain during cognitive tasks.
the estimation of the intrinsic dimension in the functional MRI space via dataset fractals analysis.
a data-driven approach for the estimation of the number of parallel processes that run in human brain activity, which is an important issue in the field of brain research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, when a specific level of activity is reached, the human brain can process information in parallel through the activation of 10 to 20 independent brain processes.
, when performing visual or visuoperceptual tasks, the brain activity in normal subjects is characterized by the simultaneous operation of 4-5 parallel independent processes.
the human brain is capable to perform complex cognitive tasks in a very efficient manner by running in parallel a large number of independent processes, in order to achieve a specific task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human brain is a highly parallel system and the number of parallel processes can be estimated by the level of activation.

the human brain is not a simple serial processor but rather a complex parallel processor with a large number of ‘cpu cores’, which are activated in different combinations for different tasks and different subjects.
we are able to estimate the level of ‘parallelism’ in brain activity and that this level can be defined as a continuous range of ‘cpu cores’.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human brain is a very complex system that can be modeled as a fractal structure and its intrinsic dimensionality can be estimated via dataset fractal and blind-source separation analysis.
the number of ‘cores’ in the human brain is not constant but varies with task difficulty.
the number of independent processes that are activated in parallel when visual tasks are performed, is much lower than the number of voxels in fMRI space.
